newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Commonwealth finds Nigeria hard nut to crack.
newsitem.headline: Commonwealth finds Nigeria hard nut to crack.

text.p: One year after suspending Nigeria for hanging nine minority rights activists, the Commonwealth is not finding it easy to push the country's military rulers into doing what it wants.
Seven Commonwealth ministers spent two days this week meeting Nigerian officials in the capital Abuja but all the negotiations had to be done on Nigeria's terms.
Diplomats said the visit was unlikely to help the Commonwealth resolve the dilemma it faced on Nigeria.

"The brinkmanship was tough and in the end the ministers went where the Nigerian government wanted them to go and heard what it wanted them to hear," said one diplomat who closely monitored the visit.
Nigeria caused worldwide outrage last November when the nine Ogoni activists including author Ken Saro-Wiwa were hanged while the Commonwealth was holding its biennial summit in New Zealand.
In the heat of the moment, the 53-member club of Britain and its former colonies unanimously agreed to suspend Nigeria.

It then set up the eight-nation Commonwealth Ministerial Action Group (CMAG) to press Nigeria to restore civil rule within two years and respect human rights in line with the Commonwealth's Harare Declaration on good governance.
Nigeria's response was defiant. It demanded that the suspension be lifted and went on an offensive against select Commonwealth members, saying they were targeting Nigeria.

Officials said military ruler General Sani Abacha made it clear to CMAG that there would be no change in the programme already being implemented to hand over to an elected president in 1998, a year later than demanded by the Commonwealth.
"The Commonwealth knows what to do about Nigeria but lacks the teeth to bite," said pro-democracy activist Alabo Isibor.

Cracks set in early among CMAG, which comprises Britain, South Africa, Canada, Malaysia, Ghana, Zimbabwe, Jamaica and New Zealand. While Canada pushed for tough action against Nigeria some called for dialogue and in the end held off imposing sanctions already agreed on.

A divide-and-rule tactic was at play in Abuja when Foreign Minister Tom Ikimi singled out Canada and Britain for what he called their "anti-Nigeria stance" and then unceremoniously freed three of many dissidents held without trial.
Nigeria has not been at peace with Western nations since June 1993 when a presidential poll to restore democracy was annulled.

Relations worsened when Moshood Abiola, a rich businessman believed to have won the vote, was detained in 1994. Despite repeated calls for his release, he has since been held pending trial for treason for declaring himself president.
Nigeria, Africa's most populous nation and rich in natural resources including oil, is extra sensitive to foreign criticisms and usually terms such action as meddling in its affairs.

At the Abuja talks, the government wheeled out dozens of traditional rulers, leaders of the five registered political parties and the electoral commission who in resplendent flowing gowns all told CMAG that the transition plan was on course.

"We told them we have confidence in the transition programme," said Lawan Gambo, chairman of the Grassroots Democratic Movement party, adding: "Nigeria must be allowed to fashion her own democracy in line with her culture and not the imposition of foreign cultures."
"Only Nigeria and Nigerians are capable and able to solve their problem,' chipped in Isa Mohammed, chairman of the United Nigeria Congress Party, the largest of the registered parties.
Not all in the nation of 250 tribes and 100 million agree.

The opposition, based mainly in the southwest, Abiola's home turf, was not allowed to meet CMAG but in memoranda they sent to the press and foreign embassies, they called for sanctions to be imposed on the country and its expulsion from the Commonwealth.
But CMAG chairman and Zimbabwean Foreign Minister Stan Mudenge appeared to rule out sanctions at the final news conference when he said: "Our committee was not set up as a sanctions committee."

CMAG member and South Africa's deputy foreign minister Azziz Pahad told BBC radio: "Ultimately, we want to see an election taking place in Nigeria where the people of Nigeria will put into power a government that enjoys their support."
The Nigerian authorities are convinced CMAG will recommend to the October 1997 summit of the Commonwealth in Edinburgh, Scotland, to lift the suspension.

"With all the information made available to them, I think they are convinced that the decision to suspend Nigeria was a mistake," said Sam Grace Ikoku, deputy chairman of the Transition Implementation Committee.
